result: RNE invagination involves basal cell area reduction (~45%), apical area increase, and basal accumulation of contractile actomyosin spanning ~15% of RNE height, resulting in cone-shaped cells with narrowing basal surfaces.
evaluation: Claims C11-C21 provide converging evidence from multiple imaging modalities (phalloidin, phosphomyosin, live markers) and quantitative measurements showing coordinated changes in cell shape and actomyosin distribution during invagination. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls and quantification (Figure 1).

result: Rockout treatment markedly reduces basal actomyosin but RNE invagination still occurs with delayed kinetics, achieving similar final basal surface area as controls, suggesting actomyosin-independent compensatory mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C22-C31 demonstrate through pharmacological perturbation, time-lapse imaging, and quantification that invagination proceeds despite reduced actomyosin. The phenotypic variability (40% severe, 30% mild) is documented with appropriate sample sizes (n=30 per experiment, N=5 experiments). The conclusion of compensation is well-supported by the observation that final basal areas are similar (C30).

result: Inhibition of proliferation reduces cell number and increases individual cell basal area, but optic cup invagination still occurs with unaffected invagination angles, indicating RNE morphogenesis can proceed with altered cell packing.
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 use established proliferation inhibitors (hydroxyurea/aphidicolin) with appropriate validation (pH3 staining, C35) and show that morphogenesis continues despite fewer, larger cells. The data support the inference that cell number influences basal area (C39) and that invagination tolerates broader basal areas (C40).

result: Rim cells exhibit directional, actin-rich lamellipodia at the basal side while maintaining apicobasal polarity and adherens junctions, representing an intermediate epithelial-mesenchymal state. This behavior persists in Rockout conditions.
evaluation: Claims C43-C55 provide detailed characterization through mosaic labeling, time-lapse imaging, and quantification of protrusive activity (C49, Figure 3D,E). The observation that rim migration continues in Rockout (C51) while invaginating cells are affected supports independence of these processes. Multiple markers (Par3, GFP-Utrophin, mKate2-ras) consistently show maintained polarity with basal protrusions.

result: Upon reaching the RNE, rim cells transition from dynamic lamellipodia formation to stable basal actomyosin enrichment, losing mesenchymal characteristics and adopting neuroepithelial morphology.
evaluation: Claims C56-C61 document a clear spatiotemporal transition in cell behavior using live imaging of actin (C58) and myosin (C59-C60) markers. The transition is well-documented through time-lapse data (Videos 5, 9) showing the change from dynamic to stable localization patterns.

result: ECM components (laminin, chondroitin sulfate, fibronectin) show differential spatial distribution, and rim cells exhibit dynamic focal adhesions (integrin, paxillin) during migration that become stable upon reaching the RNE.
evaluation: Claims C62-C68 use immunostaining and live imaging of focal adhesion markers to demonstrate spatial and temporal regulation of cell-ECM interactions. The transition from dynamic to stable focal adhesions is well-documented through time-lapse imaging (Videos 10-12) and correlates with the change in cell behavior.

result: Knockdown of laminin or opo impairs rim cell migration (reduced speed) and causes S-shaped optic cup phenotype with reduced basal actomyosin, indicating cell-ECM attachment is required for both rim migration and invagination.
evaluation: Claims C69-C78 demonstrate through morpholino knockdown, time-lapse imaging, and quantification that ECM perturbation affects both cellular processes. The phenotypic characterization is thorough with appropriate controls for knockdown efficiency (Figure 4—supplement 2) and polarity (C73-C74). The dual effect on rim migration and actomyosin accumulation (C75-C77) supports the integrated conclusion (C78).

result: In laminin and opo morphants, rim cells form blebs instead of lamellipodia and show altered paxillin dynamics (stable in laminin, transient in opo), but can still reach RNE in mosaic transplants through collective migration.
evaluation: Claims C79-C84 provide detailed cellular characterization of the morphant phenotype through live imaging and transplantation experiments. The bleb characterization (C82) includes appropriate markers (actin, myosin) to distinguish blebs from lamellipodia. The transplantation experiment (C83, N=4/5) demonstrates cell autonomy and collective migration properties.

result: Ezrin knockdown specifically induces basal blebbing in rim cells without affecting apicobasal polarity, reduces rim cell speed by 27%, causes S-shaped optic cup with minimal basal actomyosin disturbance, indicating the phenotype is primarily due to rim migration defects.
evaluation: Claims C85-C98 use ezrin knockdown as a specific perturbation of membrane-actin linkage with appropriate validation (Western blot, Figure 5—supplement 2A). The key strength is the dissociation of rim migration defects (C91) from actomyosin perturbation (C94-C95), supported by quantitative comparison of phalloidin intensity slopes (Figure 5—supplement 2E). Transplantation experiments (C89, N=2/4) show cell autonomy, though the lower success rate suggests variable knockdown efficiency.

result: Correct ECM formation is essential for lamellipodia-based rim migration; when impaired, cells form non-functional blebs and adopt neuroepithelial morphology at ectopic locations.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 synthesize findings from multiple perturbation experiments (laminin, opo, ezrin) into a coherent model. The conclusions are well-supported by the collective data showing the ECM-lamellipodia-migration axis and the consequence of its disruption.

result: Rim cells express vsx2 (RNE fate marker) only after reaching the RNE in controls, but in ezrin/laminin/opo morphants, cells that fail to migrate express vsx2 ectopically, leading to abnormal optic cup architecture persisting to 36hpf, demonstrating rim migration coordinates cell positioning with fate specification.
evaluation: Claims C102-C110 use the vsx2::GFP transgenic line to track fate specification through time-lapse imaging (Videos 20-21) and fixed samples. The ectopic expression in multiple morphant conditions (C104-C106) and persistence to neurogenesis stages (C109) strongly support the conclusion that migration timing is critical for proper fate specification and positioning (C110). The observation of secondary invagination zones (C108) provides additional evidence of the architectural consequences.

result: Active rim involution is an important driver of optic cup formation through collective epithelial migration, working together with basal constriction to shape the hemispherical RNE, with rim involution playing a dominant role as evidenced by more severe phenotypes when it is perturbed.
evaluation: Claims C111-C117 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. The dominance of rim involution (C116-C117) is supported by comparing phenotype severity across perturbations: ezrin morphants (primarily rim defects) show S-shaped cups that don't recover (C96), while Rockout (primarily invagination defects) shows milder, recoverable phenotypes (C28-C30). This comparative analysis across multiple perturbations provides strong support for the hierarchical relationship.

result: Rim cells traverse an epithelial-mesenchymal continuum, modulating behavior spatiotemporally to shape the RNE, with premature transition to stable attachment hindering organogenesis, representing a developmental strategy used across multiple stages of eye formation in teleosts.
evaluation: Claims C122-C125, C127 synthesize the cellular characterization into a conceptual framework about epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity. The spatiotemporal regulation (C125) is supported by observations that ectopically positioned cells adopt stable morphology (C97-C98, C101) and cannot be relocated. The broader developmental context (C127) is supported by cited work on earlier eye development stages (C126).

result: Rim cell migration represents a previously uncharacterized form of collective epithelial migration that occurs within a continuous epithelial sheet without leader cells but with directional lamellipodia formation, and is indispensable for proper RNE formation.
evaluation: Claims C128-C133 characterize rim migration as a distinct mode of collective migration. The lack of leader cells (C130) is supported by imaging data, and directionality without leaders (C131) is demonstrated by quantification of protrusive activity (C49, Figure 3D,E). The comparison to other systems (C130) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The indispensability (C132) is supported by the severe phenotypes when migration is perturbed.

result: Failed rim migration leads to ectopic fate specification and enduring architectural defects including secondary invagination zones, revealing that RNE fate is position-independent but proper positioning requires intact morphogenetic movements that signaling pathways alone cannot ensure.
evaluation: Claims C134-C139 integrate fate specification and morphogenesis data to demonstrate the relationship between cell positioning and developmental outcome. The position-independence of fate (C138) is directly shown by ectopic vsx2 expression (C104-C107), while the requirement for morphogenetic movements (C139) is demonstrated by the inability of fate specification to rescue positioning defects. The persistence of defects (C136) and formation of secondary zones (C137) provide strong evidence for enduring consequences.

result: Differential morphogenetic strategies for dorsal (invagination) and ventral (rim involution) retinal development are conserved across vertebrate species, with phenotypes in perturbation experiments showing ventral-temporal specificity consistent with the spatial pattern of rim involution.
evaluation: Claims C140-C145 address the spatial patterning of morphogenetic processes. The ventral-temporal specificity of phenotypes (C141-C142) is consistent with the known spatial pattern of rim involution (C140, C41). Cross-species conservation (C143-C145) is supported by appropriate citations. The inference about conserved patterning (C145) is reasonable given the comparative data, though marked as speculation in the discussion.

result: Background on RNE development: RNE is the retinal organ precursor that develops from optic vesicles through complex epithelial rearrangements including invagination and rim involution, with species-specific differences in the role of proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C1-C10 establish the developmental context through appropriate citations to prior work. These background claims are well-supported by the cited literature and provide necessary context for the study. The distinction between in vitro organoid systems (C4) and in vivo zebrafish/Xenopus (C5) appropriately motivates the study.

result: Background on proliferation and rim involution: RNE formation is accompanied by high proliferation, suggested as a driving force in vitro, but invagination persists without proliferation in zebrafish/Xenopus; rim involution relocates substantial cell numbers from proximal to distal layer, predominantly ventral-temporally.
evaluation: Claims C32-C34, C41-C42 provide additional background from the literature with appropriate citations. These establish the context for testing the roles of proliferation and rim involution in the current study.

result: Basal domain dynamics and cell-ECM interactions play important roles in various morphogenetic processes including zebrafish lateral line development, midbrain-hindbrain boundary formation, Drosophila follicle development, and in vitro optic cup organoids.
evaluation: Claims C118-C121 contextualize the findings within broader developmental biology through appropriate citations. These comparisons are well-supported by the cited literature and help position the work within the field.

result: During earlier optic vesicle evagination, eye field cells transition from mesenchymal to epithelial state by acquiring apicobasal polarity.
evaluation: Claim C126 is supported by appropriate citations (Ivanovitch et al., 2013; Bazin-Lopez et al., 2015) and provides context for the broader developmental trajectory discussed in C127.

result: Speculation that patterned morphogenesis may allow cell segregation based on environmental differences and stepwise fate acquisition, potentially conserved in organoid cultures.
evaluation: Claims C146-C147 are explicitly speculative statements about possible functions of patterned morphogenesis. While C148 cites recent work on organoids (Hasegawa et al., 2016), the functional speculation in C146-C147 lacks direct experimental support and represents hypotheses for future investigation.
